summary: This module covers the comprehensive theory, construction, performance analysis, and operational characteristics of Three-Phase Induction Motors and Synchronous Machines. In Part I (Induction Motor), it details the rotating transformer concept, production of rotating magnetic field (RMF), squirrel-cage vs. slip-ring rotor constructions, slip relations (s = (Nₛ - N) / Nₛ), rotor frequency (f' = s f), rotor electrical circuit parameters (E₂, R₂, X₂ = 2π f L₂, Z₂ = √(R₂² + X₂²)), derivation of the torque equation (T = (K s R₂ E₂²) / (R₂² + s² X₂²)), starting torque (T_st = (K R₂ E₂²) / (R₂² + X₂²)), maximum torque condition (R₂ = s X₂ ⇒ T_max = (K E₂²) / (2 X₂)), torque-slip characteristics, the power flow golden ratio (P_ir : P_cu : P_d = 1 : s : 1 - s), starting methods ((i) Direct-on-line, (ii) Stator resistance, (iii) Autotransformer, (iv) Star-delta, (v) Rotor resistance), and speed control. In Part II (Synchronous Machine), it explains the decisive advantages of stationary armature design, salient-pole vs. cylindrical smooth-rotor constructions, armature winding parameters (pitch factor Kₚ = cos(α/2), distribution factor K_d = sin(mβ/2) / [m sin(β/2)]), derivation of the alternator EMF equation (E_ph = 4.44 Kₚ K_d f Φ T), voltage regulation via the Synchronous Impedance (EMF) method (Zₛ = V_oc / I_sc, Xₛ = √(Zₛ² - Rₐ²), E₀ = √[(V cos ϕ + Iₐ Rₐ)² + (V sin ϕ ± Iₐ Xₛ)²]), synchronous motor working principle, reasons for zero starting torque, starting methods ((i) external prime mover, (ii) damper windings), V-curves and excitation effects, and synchronous condensers for substation power factor correction.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Why is a three-phase induction motor referred to as a 'rotating transformer'?
sa.a:
A 3-phase induction motor is called a rotating transformer because it works on AC through the principle of mutual induction:
(i) The stator winding acts as the primary winding, receiving 3-phase AC power and creating a rotating magnetic field in the air-gap of constant magnitude.
(ii) The rotor acts as a short-circuited secondary winding, in which EMF and circulating currents are induced by relative motion across the air gap.
(iii) Unlike a static transformer with fixed frequency, the induction motor has a rotating secondary whose induced frequency (f' = s f) varies directly with rotor slip s.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Define 'Slip' in an induction motor and write the formula for rotor current frequency.
sa.a:
(i) Synchronous Speed (Nₛ): The speed of the rotating magnetic field, given by:
Nₛ = 120 f / P  (rpm)

(ii) Slip (s): The fractional difference between synchronous speed (Nₛ) and actual rotor speed (N):
s = (Nₛ - N) / Nₛ
(At standstill N = 0, s = 1; at synchronous speed N = Nₛ, s = 0). Rotor speed is N = Nₛ(1 - s).

(iii) Rotor Current Frequency (f'): For relative speed (Nₛ - N), the rotor frequency is given by:
f' = [(Nₛ - N) P] / 120 = (s Nₛ P) / 120 = s f

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between Squirrel Cage and Slip Ring induction motors.
sa.a:
(i) Squirrel Cage Induction Motor:
- Rotor is composed of heavy copper/aluminum bars embedded in slots and shorted at both ends by end rings (resembles a squirrel cage).
- Low starting torque, high starting current, simple, low cost, robust, and low maintenance. Applications: pumps, compressors, conveyors, elevators.

(ii) Slip Ring (Wound Rotor) Induction Motor:
- Rotor winding is wound with insulated wires connected to three slip rings and brushes.
- Slip rings are short-circuited through external resistance to obtain high starting torque and smooth speed variation. Higher cost and maintenance. Applications: lifts, cranes, heavy pumps.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the condition for maximum running torque in a 3-phase induction motor and write its formula.
sa.a:
The condition for maximum running torque is obtained by differentiating the torque expression w.r.t. slip s and equating to zero:
R₂ = s X₂   or   s_m = R₂ / X₂
(i.e., Rotor resistance / phase = Fractional slip × Standstill rotor reactance / phase).

Substituting R₂ = s X₂ into the torque equation yields:
T_max = (K E₂²) / (2 X₂)
(Note: Maximum torque T_max is completely independent of rotor resistance R₂; only the slip at which it occurs is proportional to R₂).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the relation between Rotor Power Input, Rotor Copper Loss, and Mechanical Power Developed.
sa.a:
From the power flow diagram of an induction motor, power transferred across the air gap follows the golden proportion:
Rotor Power Input (P_ir) : Rotor Cu Loss (W_cu) : Mechanical Power Developed (P_d) = 1 : s : (1 - s)

Where:
(i) Rotor Cu Loss: W_cu = s × P_ir
(ii) Mechanical Power Developed: P_d = (1 - s) × P_ir = [(1 - s) / s] × W_cu
(iii) Rotor Input: P_ir = 2π Nₛ T_d / 60;  P_d = 2π N T_d / 60.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the advantages of using a Stationary Armature and Rotating Field in commercial alternators.
sa.a:
The advantages of a stationary armature are:
(i) It is easier to insulate stationary winding for high voltages (11 kV to 33 kV) because coils are not subjected to centrifugal forces and extra slot space is available.
(ii) The stationary 3-phase armature can be directly connected to the load without going through large, unreliable slip rings and brushes.
(iii) Only two slip rings are required for low-voltage DC supply to the field winding on the rotor; since exciting current is small, slip rings and brush gear are of light construction.
(iv) Due to simple and robust construction of the rotor, higher rotational speeds of rotating DC field are possible, increasing output obtainable from a machine of given dimensions.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between Salient-Pole and Cylindrical (Smooth) rotors in alternators.
sa.a:
(i) Salient-Pole Rotor:
- Projected pole type where poles project outward from the rotor surface.
- Characterized by large diameter and small axial length.
- Mechanical strength is lower; preferred for low-speed alternators (125 rpm to 500 rpm) driven by hydraulic water turbines or I.C. engines.

(ii) Smooth Cylindrical (Non-Salient Pole) Rotor:
- Smooth solid steel cylinder having slots to accommodate distributed field coils.
- Characterized by small diameter and large axial length.
- Very high mechanical strength; preferred for high-speed turbo-alternators (1500 rpm to 3000 rpm) driven by steam turbines.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Define Pitch Factor (Kₚ) and Distribution Factor (K_d) in alternator armature windings.
sa.a:
(i) Pitch Factor / Coil Span Factor (Kₚ):
The ratio of EMF induced in a short-pitch coil to the EMF induced in a full-pitch coil:
Kₚ = cos(α / 2)   (where α = short-pitch angle; Kₚ = 1 for full pitch, Kₚ < 1 for short pitch).

(ii) Distribution Factor / Breadth Factor (K_d):
The ratio of phasor sum of coil EMF/phase to arithmetic sum of coil EMF/phase:
K_d = sin(mβ / 2) / [m sin(β / 2)]
(where m = slots / pole / phase, β = slot angle = 180° / (slots/pole); K_d < 1).
Winding Factor: K_w = Kₚ × K_d.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Why is a 3-phase synchronous motor NOT self-starting?
sa.a:
A synchronous motor has no starting torque because:
(i) When 3-phase AC supply is connected to the stator, a magnetic field revolving at synchronous speed (Nₛ = 120 f / P) is produced.
(ii) At rest, the rotor possesses high mechanical inertia. During the first half-cycle, stator poles repel rotor poles (say, clockwise torque).
(iii) After a period of half-cycle (1 / (2f) = 1/100 second for 50 Hz), stator poles reverse their polarities while the heavy rotor has not moved, producing counter-clockwise torque.
(iv) Due to rapid polarity reversals, average starting torque is zero; hence the motor fails to start without auxiliary means.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is a Synchronous Condenser? State its primary industrial function.
sa.a:
A Synchronous Condenser is an over-excited synchronous motor running on no-load.

Function and Working:
(i) When over-excited (E_b > V), a synchronous motor takes a leading current (I_m leading V by angle ϕ_m) and behaves like a capacitor.
(ii) When connected in parallel with induction motors or inductive loads operating at lagging power factor cos ϕ_L, the leading kVAR supplied by the synchronous condenser neutralizes lagging reactive kVAR.
(iii) Consequently, the overall system power factor is improved from cos ϕ_L to cos ϕ. Widely used at major bulk supply substations.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of neat sketches, explain the construction and working principle of a 3-phase Induction Motor. (8 marks)
(b) Explain why an induction motor can never run at synchronous speed. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Construction and Working Principle of a 3-Phase Induction Motor:

1. Constructional Details:
(i) Stator: Laminated iron core with slots; coils are placed in slots to form a balanced 3-phase distributed winding.
(ii) Rotor: Two types:
  • Squirrel-cage Rotor: Copper/aluminum bars embedded in rotor slots and shorted at both ends by end rings (skewed to reduce humming and cogging).
  • Slip-ring (Wound) Rotor: Distributed insulated 3-phase winding connected to 3 slip rings on the shaft, allowing external resistances to be connected via brushes.

2. Working Principle:
(i) When the stator winding is connected to a 3-phase AC supply, a rotating magnetic field of constant magnitude revolving at synchronous speed Nₛ = 120 f / P is produced.
(ii) The field cuts rotor conductors, and an EMF is induced due to relative speed between rotating field and rotor conductors.
(iii) Since the rotor circuit is closed by end rings, circulating current I₂ flows in the conductors.
(iv) Current-carrying conductors placed in the magnetic field experience mechanical force (F = B I l), which in turn produces electromagnetic torque T.
(v) By Lenz's law, the rotor moves in the same direction as the rotating magnetic field in order to reduce the relative speed between them.

(b) Why an Induction Motor Can Never Run at Synchronous Speed:
(i) The torque developed is strictly dependent on induced rotor EMF (s E₂), which requires relative motion between the stator flux (Nₛ) and rotor conductors (N).
(ii) If the motor were to reach synchronous speed (N = Nₛ), the relative speed (Nₛ - N) would equal 0.
(iii) Rotor conductors would cut no flux; induced EMF would drop to zero, rotor current I₂ = 0, and driving torque T = 0.
(iv) Mechanical friction and windage would immediately decelerate the rotor to a speed slightly below synchronous speed (N < Nₛ). Hence, an induction motor must always operate with a positive slip s > 0.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Derive the expression for the torque of a 3-phase induction motor and deduce the condition for maximum running torque. (8 marks)
(b) Sketch and explain the Torque-Slip characteristics of an induction motor, highlighting starting torque, pull-out torque, and the effect of added rotor resistance. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Derivation of Induction Motor Torque & Maximum Torque Condition:

1. Torque Proportionality:
Torque developed by the rotor of an induction motor is directly proportional to:
(i) rotor current I₂
(ii) stator flux per pole Φ
(iii) power factor of rotor circuit cos ϕ₂
Therefore: T ∝ Φ I₂ cos ϕ₂
Since rotor standstill EMF E₂ ∝ Φ, we have:
T ∝ E₂ I₂ cos ϕ₂   ⇒   T = K E₂ I₂ cos ϕ₂

2. Electrical Circuit Parameters at Slip s:
- Induced EMF per phase: s E₂
- Rotor resistance per phase: R₂
- Rotor reactance per phase: s X₂ (since f' = s f)
- Rotor impedance per phase: Z₂' = √[R₂² + (s X₂)²]
- Rotor current: I₂ = (s E₂) / √[R₂² + (s X₂)²]
- Power factor: cos ϕ₂ = R₂ / √[R₂² + (s X₂)²]

3. Torque Expression:
Substituting I₂ and cos ϕ₂:
T = K E₂ × [(s E₂) / √[R₂² + (s X₂)²]] × [R₂ / √[R₂² + (s X₂)²]]
T = (K s R₂ E₂²) / (R₂² + s² X₂²)
At starting (s = 1): T_st = (K R₂ E₂²) / (R₂² + X₂²).

4. Condition for Maximum Running Torque:
To find rotor resistance giving maximum torque under running conditions, differentiate T w.r.t. s and equate to zero:
dT / ds = [K₂ R₂ (R₂² + s² X₂²) - 2s X₂² (s R₂)] / (R₂² + s² X₂²)² = 0
(R₂² + s² X₂²) - 2s² X₂² = 0
R₂² = s² X₂²   ⇒   R₂ = s X₂   (or s_m = R₂ / X₂).
Thus, for maximum running torque:
Rotor resistance / phase = Fractional slip × Standstill rotor reactance / phase.
Substituting R₂ = s X₂ into the torque equation:
T_max = (K E₂²) / (2 X₂).

(b) Torque-Slip Characteristics:
(i) At s = 0, T = 0, so the curve starts from origin.
(ii) At normal operating speed, slip is small; s² X₂² is negligible compared to R₂²: T ∝ s / R₂ ∝ s (straight line).
(iii) As slip increases beyond full load, torque reaches maximum pull-out torque at s = R₂ / X₂.
(iv) At higher slips (near standstill), s² X₂² increases rapidly and R₂² is neglected: T ∝ s / (s² X₂²) ∝ 1 / s (rectangular hyperbola).
(v) Effect of Rotor Resistance: The maximum torque T_max remains constant and independent of R₂; adding external resistance merely shifts the slip at which maximum torque occurs toward s = 1, substantially increasing starting torque.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Derive the EMF equation of an alternator, incorporating pitch factor and distribution factor. (8 marks)
(b) A 3-phase, 16-pole alternator has 144 slots with 4 conductors per slot connected in two layers. The speed is 375 rpm and flux per pole is 5 × 10⁻² Wb sinusoidally distributed. Assuming a coil span of 150° electrical, calculate the phase and line voltages. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Derivation of Alternator EMF Equation:

1. Parameters:
Let:
- Z = Number of conductors or coil sides in series per phase
- Φ = Flux per pole in Webers
- P = Number of rotor poles
- N = Rotor speed in rpm
- In one revolution (60 / N seconds), each stator conductor is cut by P Φ Webers.

2. Average EMF Induced in One Conductor:
dΦ / dt = (P Φ) / (60 / N) = (P Φ N) / 60  volts.
Since N = 120 f / P, we substitute:
Average EMF per conductor = (P Φ / 60) × (120 f / P) = 2 f Φ  volts.

3. Average and RMS EMF per Phase:
- Average EMF per phase (Z conductors in series) = 2 f Φ Z  volts.
- R.M.S. value = Average value × Form Factor (1.11 for sine wave):
  E_{r.m.s.} / phase = 2 f Φ Z × 1.11 = 2.22 f Φ Z  volts.
- In terms of turns per phase T (where Z = 2T):
  E_{r.m.s.} / phase = 4.44 f Φ T  volts.

4. Incorporating Winding Factors:
If Kₚ is the pitch factor and K_d is the distribution factor:
E_{r.m.s.} / phase = 2.22 Kₚ K_d f Φ Z  volts
E_{r.m.s.} / phase = 4.44 Kₚ K_d f Φ T  volts.

(b) Numerical Calculation:
Given Data:
- P = 16, Slots = 144, Conductors per slot = 4
- Total conductors = 144 × 4 = 576
- Conductors per phase: Z = 576 / 3 = 192
- Turns per phase: T = Z / 2 = 192 / 2 = 96 turns
- Speed N = 375 rpm  ⇒  Frequency f = (16 × 375) / 120 = 50 Hz
- Flux Φ = 5 × 10⁻² Wb
- Coil span = 150° electrical

1. Pitch Factor (Kₚ):
Chording angle: α = 180° - 150° = 30°
Kₚ = cos(α / 2) = cos(30° / 2) = cos(15°) = 0.9659

2. Distribution Factor (K_d):
Slots per pole = 144 / 16 = 9
Slot angle: β = 180° / (Slots/pole) = 180° / 9 = 20°
Slots per pole per phase: m = 144 / (16 × 3) = 3
K_d = sin(mβ / 2) / [m sin(β / 2)] = sin(3 × 20° / 2) / [3 sin(20° / 2)] = sin(30°) / [3 sin(10°)] = 0.5000 / [3 × 0.17365] = 0.9598

3. Phase and Line Voltage:
E_ph = 4.44 × Kₚ × K_d × f × Φ × T
E_ph = 4.44 × 0.9659 × 0.9598 × 50 × (5 × 10⁻²) × 96 = 987.88 V  (Ans)
Line Voltage V_L = √3 × E_ph = √3 × 987.88 = 1711.06 V  (Ans)

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the determination of voltage regulation of an alternator by the Synchronous Impedance (EMF) Method. (8 marks)
(b) Describe the starting methods of synchronous motors using: (i) an external prime mover, and (ii) damper windings. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Voltage Regulation by Synchronous Impedance (EMF) Method:

1. Definition:
Voltage regulation is the increase in terminal voltage expressed as percentage of full-load terminal voltage when load at a given power factor is thrown off, with speed and field current remaining constant:
% Voltage regulation = [(E₀ - V) / V] × 100

2. Factors Affecting Voltage Regulation:
(i) Iₐ Rₐ drop in armature winding
(ii) Iₐ X_L drop in armature winding
(iii) Voltage change due to armature reaction

3. Method of Determination:
(i) Armature resistance Rₐ per phase: Measured by DC voltmeter-ammeter method; effective AC resistance Rₐ = 1.5 R_dc (skin effect).
(ii) Open-circuit characteristic (O.C.C.): Alternator run at rated speed; open-circuit phase terminal voltage plotted against field current I_f.
(iii) Short-circuit characteristic (S.C.C.): Terminals short-circuited; short-circuit armature current I_sc plotted against I_f.

4. Calculation of Zₛ and Xₛ:
Zₛ = E_rated(from open circuit) / I_sc(from short circuit test) = V_oc / I_sc
Xₛ = √(Zₛ² - Rₐ²)

5. Phasor Equation for Generated EMF E₀:
E₀ = √[(V cos ϕ + Iₐ Rₐ)² + (V sin ϕ ± Iₐ Xₛ)²]
(+ sign for lagging power factor, - sign for leading power factor, ϕ = 0 for unity power factor).
Once E₀ is evaluated, % Voltage regulation = [(E₀ - V) / V] × 100.

(b) Methods of Self-Starting of Synchronous Motor:
(i) Motor Starting with an External Prime Mover:
  • An auxiliary motor or prime mover rotates rotor poles to synchronous speed in clockwise direction.
  • After a period of half-cycle, stator poles and rotor poles interchange positions, maintaining unidirectional torque.
  • Magnetic interlocking occurs between stator and rotor poles, pulling the rotor into synchronism. The external prime mover is then decoupled.
(ii) Motor Starting with Damper Windings:
  • Damper winding consists of copper bars embedded in salient pole faces and short-circuited at both ends.
  • (i) 3-phase supply is given to stator with rotor field unenergized; rotating stator field induces currents in damper bars, starting motor as an induction motor.
  • (ii) As rotor approaches synchronous speed, field is excited with direct current. Rotor poles lock in with rotating stator poles.
  • (iii) At synchronous speed, damper bars cut no flux and carry no current, dropping out of operation automatically.
